description: Equipo huixtleco que tiene como objetivo demostrar lo que queda a imaginación y posibilidad al futuro del planeta
summary:
The project is an interactive application designed to explore Mars in an immersive and accurate way. It integrates real-time scientific data—such as location telemetry, atmospheric temperature, and wind speed—with detailed maps that allow users to plot routes across the Red Planet’s most iconic landmarks, including Olympus Mons and Jezero Crater.

The app addresses the challenge of translating complex, scattered space data into an intuitive and accessible visual experience. By combining live environmental monitoring with cartographic navigation, it transforms technical mission data into a practical tool for exploration.

Its importance lies in democratizing scientific knowledge and inspiring future generations of astronomers and engineers. Beyond serving as an engaging educational resource, it lays the conceptual groundwork for future navigation and route-planning tools in extraterrestrial environments
details:
What does it do and how does it work? It is an interactive planetary exploration app that collects and displays real-time scientific data from Mars. It connects to public space APIs (such as NASA's) to pull live updates on temperature, wind speed, atmospheric pressure, and active rover locations. Additionally, it features an interactive map that lets users plot custom routes and explore iconic Martian landmarks like Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, and Jezero Crater.

What are its benefits?

  • Easy-to-understand science: Turns complex, raw data from space missions into simple visuals and maps anyone can read.
  • Hands-on learning: Promotes STEM education (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math) through visual exploration rather than static textbook reading.
  • All-in-one platform: Combines live Martian weather tracking and route mapping in a single, user-friendly interface.

What is the expected impact of the project? The main goal is to make space knowledge accessible to everyone and inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers. In the short term, it serves as a dynamic educational tool for students and space enthusiasts. In the long term, it acts as an early prototype for the navigation and weather-monitoring systems that future astronauts will need on Mars.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend (User Interface): HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (or frameworks like React / Flutter) to build a smooth, responsive design.
  • Backend & Data: Python or Node.js to fetch and organize real-time data from NASA’s open APIs (like the Mars Weather Service and rover telemetry).
  • Maps & Geolocation: Mapping libraries such as Leaflet, Mapbox, or CesiumJS paired with Martian topographic maps (MOLA / HiRISE).
  • Design & Collaboration: Figma for designing the layout (UX/UI) and Git/GitHub for version control.

How is your project creative? Its creativity lies in taking complex astronomical data—usually hidden in technical tables—and presenting it like an everyday Earth app (similar to Google Maps or a local weather app), but built for another planet. Blending familiar navigation tools with space exploration makes Mars feel close, real, and easy to explore.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Ease of use (UX): Keeping the design clean and intuitive so anyone can use it without needing a background in astronomy.
  • Data accuracy and delays: Using reliable scientific sources and accounting for communication delays when receiving live updates from Mars.
  • App performance: Optimizing high-resolution maps so the app loads quickly and runs smoothly on both computers and mobile devices.
